title: K-Drama Teach You a Lesson Joins Netflix's All-Time Top 10, Beating Squid Game's Hype
text:
A K-drama has finally joined Netflix's all-time Top 10, and it's not Squid Game. Teach You a Lesson, a South Korean series, has amassed 63.4 million views and has been a Weekly Top 10 for nine weeks, with many at #1. The show's success is a testament to the enduring popularity of K-dramas and their ability to tackle complex social issues. Teach You a Lesson's bold premise and thoughtful social commentary have resonated with audiences, making it a standout series in a competitive season. The show's portrayal of the Education Rights Protection Bureau's agents is particularly noteworthy, as they serve as a commentary on the failures of the education system and the need for reform. Overall, Teach You a Lesson is a thought-provoking and entertaining series that offers a unique perspective on the challenges facing South Korea's education system.
In the fall of 2021, Netflix had over 220 million subscribers worldwide as its captive audience under once-in-a-lifetime unusual circumstances. The world had watched plenty of reruns from The Office and devoured the Tiger King, and while plenty of audiences discovered anime in that era, another explosive burst in interest emerged with K-dramas thanks to the impossibly dominant debut of Squid Game.
The series and its three seasons sit handily at the top of Netflix's Most Popular Non-English Shows of All Time scoreboard, with season 1 in particular meeting the 91-day debut window criteria easily, with 265.2 million views, and 2.2 billion hours watched. To say the world was enamored with Squid Game and its cast of actors, many of whom rotating with other ongoing K-drama hits, would be a vast understatement.
But while plenty of audience members misunderstood the premise, instead craving the dark spins on childhood games with macabre fates for the losers, this additional appeal only served to boost the profile of the series. It led to various attempts to capitalize on Squid Game's appeal, but it also presented a daunting challenge to all shows, K-dramas or otherwise, to try and meet its hype.
Nothing has ever replicated the conditions to match Squid Game's debut or even that of its subsequent seasons. But some, thanks in no small part to tackling taboo subjects and bearing some social commentary of their own, were able to chart similarly. Now, one other K-drama has meaningfully joined Netflix's all-time Top 10, and it's worth diving into.
Only One Other K-Drama Sits With Squid Game On Netflix's Top 10 Close It took five years, but even meeting a fraction of Squid Game's success is a daunting challenge even for the dominant K-drama medium on Netflix. While there are no other shows of this type on the Non-English charts, that is not to say K-dramas are by any means less popular; they are incredibly saturated on the platform, and they are increasingly consistent in representing South Korea's cultural output compared to virtually any other market.
So, when Teach You a Lesson amassed 63.4 million views without still even being out for 91 days, eventually running for nine solid Weekly Top 10s with many at #1, it scored #10 on the all-time Netflix charts. This presented a satisfying new feat, bookending the chart for South Korea with weeks to spare for its run.
In fact, for all of 2026 so far, K-dramas have continued to flood public discourse, with Teach You a Lesson's absurd premise sparking plenty of discussion on its special government entity authorized to use corporal and/or other creative punishment to subdue students, teachers, and abusive parents. With its star, Kim Mu-yeol, an established action and thriller actor, and Netflix's audiences being demonstrably obsessed with the genre, Teach You a Lesson mixed in elements of these genres with a healthy dose of comedy to offset its most controversial elements.
It's been received particularly well even in a competitive season packed with other hit K-dramas produced by Netflix or licensed by the platform. But perhaps what's most compelling about seeing Teach You a Lesson do well enough to meet even a chart-worthy fraction of Squid Game's success, is in how it wraps up its bold premise in some thoughtful social commentary.
Teach You A Lesson & Squid Game Are Wildly Different Yet Attractively Bold Controversial depictions of violence in political, economical, or social allegory isn't particularly new and isn't even exclusive to South Korea, but much like revenge cinema, the country's finest filmmakers in TV and movies have mastered them. Whether it's cases like Japan's Battle Royale or Korea's Squid Game, death game fiction has worked well because of the heavy-handed messaging it delivers about generational conflict and economic inequality, respectively.
Squid Game has a message to say, particularly in season 1, and the grim choices made by people in desperate financial situations make it darkly compelling to watch, even if the spectacle sometimes overtakes the themes. By comparison, Teach You a Lesson almost feels tongue-in-cheek compared to the commentary it throws down, but it's still shockingly poignant. The solutions proposed by the fictional Education Rights Protection Bureau's agents in this series range from direct retribution, to outright jailing students.
The series tackles bullying driving some students to suicide with unsettling shots of witnesses of roof-jumpers watching the blood pool near their shoes. It features teachers leveraging public goodwill while secretly thumbing the scales for undeserving students. Parents are shown pushing their students past their breaking points to achieve impossibly high standards. It showcases a multifaceted problem hitting on all levels of the education system.
The series' social commentary ties into the bleak reality of South Korea's education system, where the pressure to succeed can be suffocating for young students. This theme is particularly resonant in Teach You a Lesson, which highlights the consequences of a system that prioritizes results over individual well-being. The show's portrayal of the Education Rights Protection Bureau's agents is also noteworthy, as they serve as a commentary on the failures of the education system and the need for reform.
Overall, Teach You a Lesson is a thought-provoking and entertaining series that offers a unique perspective on the challenges facing South Korea's education system. It's a testament to the power of K-dramas to tackle complex social issues and spark meaningful conversations
